5.71.m: The glorious Devī said: / O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, Inner Self of all, Source of everything, / Lord of gods, Mahādeva, omniscient one, mine of compassion!
I have indeed been favored by you; speak again out of compassion. / The mantras that enchant the three worlds were spoken to me by you, O Lord.
Tell me this: in what particular ways did that god, / of vastly enchanting form, sport with the cowherd maidens?
Mahādeva said: / Once, playing his vīṇā, Nārada, the best of sages, / learning of Kṛṣṇa's descent, went to Nanda's Gokula.
Going there to the house of Nanda, he saw the Lord, the all-pervading, imperishable one, / embodied in great yoga, performing the drama of a child;
lying upon a golden couch covered with a very soft cloth, / gazed upon with continuous delight by the daughters of cowherds;
having extremely delicate limbs, charming, with a charming gaze, / with his circlet of dark, curling locks falling loose around him;
revealing one or two budding teeth with the sprout of a slight smile, / illuminating the interior of the house all around with his own radiance.
Beholding him clad in the directions, he felt immense joy. / Conversing with Nanda, the lord of cowherds, he who is beloved by the Lord of all said:
“The life of those devoted to Nārāyaṇa is exceedingly rare to attain. / None in this world know his incomparable majesty.
Even Śiva, Brahmā, and others desire eternal delight in him; / and the sports of this child bring joy to all.
Those like them, with minds full of love, joyfully sing, / listen to, and celebrate this son of yours of unfathomable majesty.”
such men exist, and for them there will be no obstacle in worldly existence. / Abandon here all desires for the other world, O best of cowherds;
show love to this boy exclusively, with single-minded devotion.” / Having spoken thus, that best of sages went out from Nanda's dwelling.
Worshiped by him with the thought of Viṣṇu, bowed to, and dismissed, / then that great devotee of the Lord, the sage, reflected:
“His beloved, the divine Lakṣmī, in the presence of Nārāyaṇa, Hari, / assuming the form of a cowherd woman for the sport of the bow-bearing Lord,
has surely descended; of this there is no doubt. / I shall search for her today in house after house of the inhabitants of Vraja.”
Reflecting thus, the best of sages, having become a guest, / entered the dwellings of the inhabitants of Vraja, well-worshiped with the thought of Viṣṇu.
Seeing the supreme love of all the cowherds and others for Nanda's son, / the best of sages bowed to them all in his mind.
In the house of the cowherds he saw a girl of white form; / seeing her, he reflected: “This indeed is Ramā, no doubt.”
Then the wise [sage] entered the great house of a certain foremost cowherd / named Bhānu, a great-souled friend of Nanda.
Worshiped according to rule by him, that great-minded [sage] asked him: / “O virtuous one, you are renowned on earth for your devotion to dharma;
I observe your abundance of wealth, grain, and the like. / Do you have a worthy son, or a daughter of auspicious marks,
by whom your fame will pervade the entire world?” / Being addressed thus by the best of sages, Bhānu brought his little son,
greatly energetic and proud, and had him bow to Nārada. / Seeing him, who was matchless on earth in beauty,
with broad eyes like lotus petals, a fine neck, charming eyebrows, / lovely teeth, lovely ears, and beautiful in every limb,
embracing him with his arms and shedding tears of affection, / the great sage then spoke with affection, his voice faltering:
Nārada said: / “This child of yours will become a close friend of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; / untiring, he will sport with the two of them day and night.”
Then, having addressed that best of cowherds, when the foremost sage / made up his mind to go, Bhānu spoke to him thus:
“O lord, I have a daughter, like the wife of a god, / younger than this child, having the appearance of one inert, blind, and deaf.
Out of eagerness for her growth, I beg a boon of you, O most venerable one: / by a mere gracious glance, make the girl sound.”
Having heard Nārada's speech thus, his mind drawn by curiosity, / then entering the house and picking up the daughter rolling on the ground,
placing her in his lap, his mind overwhelmed with affection, / Bhānu came near the best of sages, bent with devotion.
Then the foremost devotee, the sage who is very dear to Kṛṣṇa, / seeing her supreme form, unseen, unheard of, wonderful,
the great sage, loving Hari, was enchanted as never before, / plunging into the ocean of supreme bliss, the singular elixir.
For two muhūrtas there the sage was like a stone; / then, regaining consciousness, the lord of sages slowly opened his eyes.
Filled with great astonishment, he remained silent; / in his inner heart, the greatly wise one thought in this manner:
“I have wandered through all the worlds, roaming at my own will, / and never anywhere have I seen one equal in beauty to her.
My movement extends to the world of Brahmā, the world of Rudra, and the world of Indra; / not even a ten-millionth part of her beauty has been seen anywhere.
The divine Mahāmāyā has been seen, the daughter of the king of mountains, / by whose beauty all the mobile and immobile universe is bewildered;
even she, delicate in limbs, never attains the beauty of this girl. / Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Kānti, Vidyā, and other noble women—
not even their shadow touches hers; it is never seen. / The form of Mohinī assumed by Viṣṇu, by which Hara was enchanted,
was also seen by me; how could it be equal to this girl's? / Therefore, I have no capacity whatsoever to know her true nature,
and others too mostly do not know this beloved of Hari. / Simply from beholding her, at Govinda's lotus feet,
the swelling of love that arose in me has never occurred before. / Exclusively, I praise you who display immense sovereignty;
her form is suited for the supreme delight of Kṛṣṇa.” / Reflecting thus, the sage, having sent the foremost cowherd somewhere,
in secret praised the girl of divine form: / “O goddess, O ruler of the great Yogamāyā, O one of great splendour,
O one of divine limbs greatly bewildering, O one showering great sweetness, / O one whose mind is relaxed in the bliss of the wondrous rasa,
by some great good fortune you have come into the path of my sight! / Your gaze, O goddess, is perceived to be turned constantly inward;
within yourself indeed you appear fully satisfied in great bliss. / This gracious, sweet, gentle ornament that is your fair face
manifests an indescribable, wondrous arising of inner joy! / The bud-like power connected with rajas, in terms of reality, O supremely radiant one,
you abide as that which takes the form of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; / you are the supreme reality, the supreme power of knowledge of pure sattva,
bearing the supreme mass of bliss, the supreme state belonging to Viṣṇu. / Who are you, O one of wondrous power, unapproachable by Brahmā, Rudra, and others?
You never touch the path of meditation of the lords of yoga. / The power of will, the power of knowledge, and the power of action of your Lord,

are only a portion of you—such is the thought that arises in my mind. / The inconceivable glories of Māyā belong to the supreme Lord, Mahāviṣṇu, the master of Māyā who acts like a child; / all of them are merely parts of your parts.
You are the power whose very form is bliss, O sovereign goddess, there is no doubt; / and with you Kṛṣṇa surely sports in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Even with your youthful form you bewilder the universe;
what must your wondrous form be like when touched by the age of youth? / What kind of loveliness is yours, accompanied by playful smiles and glances?
Assuming a human body for Hari, a form adorned with wonder, / I desire to see that form of yours, O beloved of Hari,
by which Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, will become utterly enchanted! / Now, out of compassion for me, O great goddess,
you ought to reveal your own form to me who am bowed and surrendered!” / Addressed thus by the best of sages, with his mind following his vow,
having bowed to the great sovereign goddess, supreme and full of great bliss, / her limbs trembling with longing from great love, fair-eyed,
as he looked upon her, he stood praising Govinda in this manner: / “Victory, O Kṛṣṇa, enchanter of the mind! Victory, O lover of Vṛndāvana!
Victory, charming with knitted eyebrows! Victory, engrossed in the sound of the flute! / Victory, adorned with peacock feathers! Victory, enchanter of the cowherd maidens!
Victory, whose limbs are smeared with saffron! Victory, adorned with jewels! / When, by your grace, accompanied by her of divine form,
with the splendour of a body charming in fresh youth, / shall I behold you, the enchanter in early youth, O Lord of the universe?”
Even as he was praising thus, from that very moment she again / became possessed of a divine form, supremely enchanting,
corresponding to the age of fourteen years, supremely graceful; / and at that very moment other cowherd girls appeared of equal age.
having arrived, they encircled [her], adorned with divine ornaments, garments, and garlands. / But that lord of sages became motionless, stunned with wonder.
Then those companions of the girl, having sprinkled the sage / with drops of water from her feet, awakened him and, filled with compassion, said:
"O best of sages, highly fortunate one, lord of great masters of yoga! / Surely, by you alone with supreme devotion has the Lord, the divine Hari,
been worshipped, the god who fulfills the desires of devotees, / since she, who is difficult to see and difficult to reach even by gods such as Brahmā and Rudra,
and by masters of the Siddhas and sages, and by other great devotees of the Lord— / this enchantress of wondrous youth and beauty, the beloved of Hari—
has entered your range of vision through some unthinkable good fortune. / Arise, arise, O brahmin sage! Quickly summon your fortitude!
Having circumambulated her, bow down to her again and again. / Do you not see the lovely-limbed girl, who seems utterly agitated?
In this very moment, surely, she will disappear. / By no means will any conversation with her take place for you,
nor will you behold her again, O best knower of Brahman! / But in Vṛndāvana there shines a certain auspicious aśoka vine,
rich in flowers in all seasons, its fragrance pervading all quarters, / not far from Govardhana, on the bank of the lake called Kusuma.
At its root, at midnight, you will see all of us without exception." / Having heard these words of theirs, whose minds were overwhelmed with affection,
just as the sage, having circumambulated her, bowed down like a staff / for two muhūrtas before the girl, who was adorned with various creations,
having called [Vṛṣa]bhānu, Nārada spoke of her, the all-fair one: / "This girl possesses such power; she cannot be attained even by gods.
Moreover, in whichever house is adorned with her footprints, / there the god Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, dwells in person;
and Lakṣmī constantly dwells there with all her supernatural powers. / Guard today in your house with effort, O best of men,
this fair-hipped girl adorned with all ornaments, like the supreme goddess!" / Having said this, the best among great devotees of the Lord, with his mind alone
remembering that very form of hers, entered the dense forest. / Having approached the root of the aśoka vine, that best of sages,
awaiting that goddess's arrival right there at night, / stayed there, agitated with love, contemplating the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, at the stroke of midnight, [he saw] exceedingly wonderful maidens, / those seen previously and others, adorned with diverse ornaments and garlands.
Having seen [them], bewildered in mind, he fell on the ground like a staff. / Surrounding the sage, all those auspicious maidens approached.
Though desiring to ask something dear to his heart, that sage / could not speak, overpowered by love, charm, and endearing speech.
Then, having approached the best of sages, who stood with folded hands, / his neck bowed with the weight of devotion, filled with wonder and awe,
the exceedingly humble one was addressed right there, with compassion, / by the deity of the aśoka grove named Aśokamālinī.
Aśokamālinī said: / "O great sage, I reside in the bud of this aśoka [vine], / always wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and red ointments,
wearing a bud of red vermilion, adorned with a red water-lily as an ear-ornament, / embellished with ruby armlets, a diadem, and the like.
Once, during the spring festival, sporting with [Hari's] beloved, / cowherd girls in multicolored garments met right there.
And with garlands of aśoka, I worshipped Hari who bore the guise of a cowherd, / and all those [maidens] who possessed the form of Ramā, with proper devotion.
Ever since, having pleased the Lord of Ramā with diverse ornaments, / I always remain in their midst.
I know completely everything here, from the highest to the lowest; / and I also know the secret of the cows, cowherds, cowherd maidens, and the rest.
Everything inquired about by you has been reflected in my heart: / 'That goddess of wondrous form, who bestows wonderful bliss,
the beloved of Hari, possessing the luster of gold, with a ring flashing with diamonds— / how may I see that trembling-eyed one, or how [may I behold] her lotus feet?'
" 'She is worshipped with great devotion'—thus has been contemplated by you, O brahmin. / Concerning that, I shall tell you the account of very great-souled ones,
who, having stayed at the Mānasa lake, undertook severe penance, / chanting perfected mantras and meditating upon Hari, the Lord—
sages constantly yearning for her very lotus feet, / numbering seventy-one thousand, endowed with great fiery power.
That supreme secret in the forest I shall now tell you."

5.72.m: The Lord said: / "Having fixed your mind on that alone, listen, O goddess of fair face! / There was a sage named Ugratapas, firm in his vows.
Maintaining the sacred fires and feeding on fire, he performed exceedingly wondrous penance. / He chanted the supreme fifteen-syllable mantra to be muttered,
enclosed by the kāma-mantra, granting desires at will, / the word 'kṛṣṇāya' combined with 'svāhā', bestowing the supreme perfection.
And he meditated on the dark-complexioned Kṛṣṇa, maddened by the rāsa-dance, eager for the best [pleasures], / wearing yellow silk, holding a flute placed to his lower lip with his hand,
endowed with fresh youth, drawing his beloved with his hand. / Thus devoted to meditation, casting off his body at the end of a hundred kalpas,
that great sage became the daughter of a cowherd named Sunanda, / renowned as Sunandā, holding a lute in her hand.
Another sage, famous as Satyatapas, of great vows, / who ate only dry leaves, muttered the supreme mantra,
ten syllables ending with 'rati' and enclosed by the kāma seed-syllable. / That best of sages meditated intensely upon Hari wearing wondrous attire,
holding the two creeper-like arms of Ramā, flashing with bracelets, / dancing, maddening [her], and embracing her again and again,
laughing aloud, a wave of bliss, holding the flute / upon his garment at his belly, resplendent with the Vaijayantī garland down to his knees,
his turned face having its forehead bathed with drops of sweat. / Casting off body after body through penance, that great sage,
after ten kalpas, was born here from the Nanda grove / as the daughter, famed as Bhadrā, of a cowherd named Subhadra,
on whose back a divine fan is seen. / There was another great sage named Haridhāman.
He too performed severe austerities, daily eating only leaves; / he muttered the twenty-syllabled mantra that quickly grants accomplishment.
Thereafter, mounted upon the kāma seed-syllable, / māyā before it, the ether, haṃsa, blood, luster, and moon;
then the ten-syllable [mantra] followed by 'namas', beginning with smara and the rest. / He meditated upon the Lord in delightful Vṛndāvana in a bower of mādhavī,
lying facing upward on a beautiful bed of sprouts, / by a certain cowherd maiden deeply tormented by passion, with red eyes,
covering his broad chest again and again with her pair of breasts, / whose cheek-edge was being kissed, whose lower lip was being savored,
drawing his beloved with his arms, smiling, joyful, and wondrous. / And that sage, having discarded many bodies, after three kalpas,
became the daughter of a cowherd named Sāraṅga, endowed with auspicious marks, / renowned as Raṅgaveṇī, skilled in the art of painting.
On whose teeth painted red drops are seen. / A certain sage, an expounder of Brahman known as Jābāli,
Devoted to austerities, a yogin wandering this earth, / In a great forest ten thousand yojanas broad,
Went by chance and saw an exceedingly beautiful stepped well, / Its banks bound with crystal on every side, filled with sweet water,
Caressed by breezes carrying the fragrance of blooming lotuses. / On its western side, at the root of a banyan tree,
He saw a certain female ascetic performing severe tapas, / Endowed with youthful age, exceedingly charming in form,
With a radiance like moonbeams, adorned in all her limbs, / Having placed her left hand on the slope of her hip, and then with her right
Displaying the mudrā of wisdom, with unblinking eyes, / Having renounced food and diversion, standing entirely motionless.
Desiring to know her, the best of sages stood there for a hundred years. / At the end of that, having raised her as she moved, the sage out of modesty
Asked: 'Who are you of wondrous form? What are you about to do? / If it is fitting, you should kindly tell me.'
Then the girl, severely emaciated by tapas, slowly said: / 'I am the peerless Brahmavidyā, sought after by the lords of yogins.
Desiring the lotus feet of Hari, for a very long time / I have been performing tapas in this dreadful forest, meditating on the Supreme Person.
Though I am filled with the bliss of Brahman, my intellect satisfied with that bliss, / Still I consider myself empty without love for Kṛṣṇa.
Now, deeply despondent, the abandonment of this body / I wish to perform right here, in this sacred stepped well.'
Hearing those words of hers, the sage was utterly amazed. / Falling at her feet, the auspicious method of worshiping Kṛṣṇa
He asked, filled with supreme joy, having cast aside philosophical discourse. / Having understood the mantra spoken by her, he went to Lake Mānasa.
Then he performed wondrous, exceedingly arduous tapas: / Standing on one foot, looking unblinkingly at the sun,
He muttered the supreme twenty-five-syllable mantra. / With supreme devotion, he meditated upon Kṛṣṇa whose form is bliss,
Roaming in the alleys of Vraja with playful, wondrous gaits, / Making his anklets tinkle with graceful placements of his feet,
With wondrous love-like gestures, with smiling, sidelong glances, / With his flute named Saṃmohana, wondrous with its reddish fifth note,
Kissing the cavity of his bimba-like lips, enchanting with soft notes, / Stealing away the minds and bodies of the women of Vraja,
His limbs suddenly embraced by them as they came with loosened skirts, / Wearing celestial garlands and garments, anointed with celestial fragrant paste,
Enchanting the three worlds with the abundant luster of his dark limbs. / Having thus worshipped the Lord of the world with much devotion,
At the interval of nine kalpas, he was born in Gokula in a divine form, / As the daughter of a very renowned cowherd named Pracaṇḍa,
A fair-faced maiden known as Citragandhā, / Gladdening the ten directions with the diverse perfumes of her own limbs.
Behold that auspicious girl drinking honey in groups, / Having made her own husband upon her limbs, agitated by the onset of aesthetic relish.
In the embrace of her breasts, he is struck by all the necklaces / Slipping from her bosom, and by the varied fragrances and other sweet scents.
Other excellent sages, their minds constantly purified, / Subsisting on air, performed tapas while muttering the supreme mantra:
'To Kāma, to Kṛṣṇa, who possesses love-distressed artistic skill and other states,' / Adding the Agni-seed syllable to the fifteen-syllable mantra.
The best of sages meditated upon Kṛṣṇa's form with divine ornaments, / Its full, plump hip-region clad in celestial, variegated silk,
With a crest arranged with peacock feathers, with radiant earrings, / Drawing the right lotus foot near the left shank,
Wandering about, folding his two lovely lotus hands, / With his flute tucked into his armpit, with lips softly moving,
Delighting the eyes and minds of the cowherd women, / Having entered the dance pavilion in an exceedingly wondrous form,
And being showered on all sides with rains of flowers by the cowherd women. / Then, having cast off their bodies at the end of a kalpa, they were born here now,
On whose ears ear-rings illuminated with beams of light are seen, / Jewel garlands on their necks, and jewel flowers in their braids.
A sage named Śuciśravas, and another named Suvarṇa, / Both sons of the brahmin sage Kuśadhvaja, masters of the Vedas,
Performed fierce tapas with feet raised, / Muttering with controlled minds the three-syllable mantra: 'Hrīṃ, Haṃsaḥ!'
Meditating upon Kṛṣṇa in Gokula as a ten-year-old boy, / With a form equal to Kāma, and charming with youthfulness,
Constantly enchanting the bimba-lipped women of Vraja who gazed upon him. / At the end of the kalpa, having discarded their bodies, those two attained birth in Vraja
As the exceedingly beautiful daughters of the cowherd named Suvīra, / In whose hands are seen two sweetly singing female parrots.
Jaṭila, Jaṅghāpūta, Ghṛtāśin, and Karbura— / Four blessed sages free from desires in this world and the next—
Taking refuge in the Lord of the cowherdesses with an undivided mind, / Performed tapas submerged in water, muttering the mantra

Beginning with 'Smara' and ending with the ten-syllable phrase, enveloped with three Lakṣmī-seeds. / And with intense devotion they meditated on him wandering from forest to forest with the cowherdesses,
Honoring them with dances, songs, and the like—the charming one, / All his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, wearing a hibiscus flower as an ear ornament,
Encircled with a garland of white water lilies, clad in blue and yellow garments. / At the end of three kalpas, they were born in Gokula, endowed with auspicious marks.
These are those charming ones seated before us, with arched eyebrows, / On whose forearms are bracelets formed out of merit,
Variegated with jewels and divine pearls. / A sage named Dīrghatapas became Vyāsa in a previous kalpa.
His son was known as the sage Śuka, excellent and wise. / Even as a boy, highly intelligent, constantly remembering the feet [of the Lord],
Abandoning parents and relatives, meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, he went to the forest. / There, with divine mental services day and night,
Without food, he worshiped Viṣṇu, the Lord in the form of a cowherd, / Muttering the eighteen-syllable mantra enveloped with the Lakṣmī-seed.
With supreme devotion he meditated on Hari beneath a golden tree, / Inside a golden pavilion, upon a golden throne,
Seated, holding a golden flute with the tips of his golden hands, / Twirling a golden lotus with his right hand,
His body painted with designs by his golden-complexioned beloved, / Smiling with great joy, looking at his own hermitage.

Filled with tears of joy, his limbs bristling with horripilation, saying aloud, 'Be pleased, O Lord!' / Trembling, he fell to the ground in a prostration like a staff before the Creator of the three worlds.
Seeing him desiring devotion, fallen upon the earth, crying out, 'I am exhausted!' / [Hari] took hold of the arms of him who lay prostrate like a staff and touched him with eyes filled with joy,
And Hari spoke to Śuka, who had attained the form of a beloved: / 'You are my most beloved, O auspicious one; always remain near me.'
“And meditating upon my form, she has attained the abode of love. / There are two foremost cowherd women, equal in age and auspicious,
having the same vows, the same devotion, and names of the same asterism. / One is renowned as like molten gold; right there, the other has the splendor of lightning.
One has eyes that seem sleepy, the other has gentle, long eyes. / With supreme devotion, she worshipped those two on Hari’s left and right.
At the end of the cosmic age, she cast off her body and became in Gokula / the daughter of the high-souled Upananda, with the beauty of a blue lotus petal.
She is that very woman of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, clad in a yellow garment, / fully dressed in a red bodice, with breasts like golden jars,
wearing red vermilion, with a veil over her entire body, / her cheek-region radiant with golden earrings, exceedingly beautiful,
adorned with a garland of golden lotuses, her lovely breasts anointed with saffron; / in her hand is seen an offering of betel given by Hari.
Exceedingly skilled in playing the flute, an attendant of Keśava, / by Kṛṣṇa, who was well pleased with her singing at one time,
an auspicious garland of guñjā seeds was placed around her conch-like neck, and it shines brightly. / Even in Kṛṣṇa's absence, afflicted by love, [she shines] with splendor.
While her female friends play instruments, singing exceedingly well in supreme voice, / having dressed this young woman in the dress of her beloved, he makes her dance.
Again and again, lovingly embracing Govinda, she kisses him. / She is beloved to all the cowherd women, and also exceedingly dear to Kṛṣṇa.”
There was a certain son of Śvetaketu, a master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, / who, abandoning everything, undertook severe ascetic penance.
The feet of Murāri being served, sounding sweet as nectar, / the beloved power of Govinda, inaccessible even to Brahmā, Rudra, and others,
serving her with singular devotion, charming Śrī herself, / constantly meditating, he recited the eleven-syllable mantra.
[Thinking,] "Having made all smiling, uniting them in the divine play, / with laughs and splendid virtues perfuming the entire world,
abide in spring," thus always contemplating the meaning of the mantra, / he too, attained perfection in just two cosmic ages and obtained birth here.
She acts as this young maiden, a daughter, slender-limbed, with budding breasts, / her neck gleaming with a string of pearls, wearing pure silk,
adorned with pearl-inlaid anklets, bracelets, armlets, and finger-rings, / wearing two divine, auspicious earrings that pour forth nectar,
bearing a mark on her forehead resembling a drop of vermilion in the middle of a rounded musk braid, / along with decorative marks of sandalwood.
She indeed is seen here, tranquil, muttering the supreme state. / There was a royal sage named Candraprabha, pleasant to behold;
by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, he had a son of sweet form, / known as Citradhvaja, who was a Vaiṣṇava from his boyhood.
That king instructed his gentle, steadfast son, twelve years of age, / into the supreme eighteen-syllable mantra from a twice-born guru.
Being consecrated with the nectar-filled waters of the mantra, / that child, bowing with love to the king at that moment, was filled with tears.
On that day, that boy, wearing pure garments, pure himself, / adorned with necklaces, anklets, cords, neck-ornaments, armlets, and bracelets,
devoted to Hari, of spotless heart, / went to the temple of Viṣṇu, and staying alone, contemplated:
“How shall I worship that lover, the deluder of the cowherd women, / who constantly sports with them in the forest on the bank of the Kālindī?”
While the boy was thus contemplating with a deeply agitated mind, / he then obtained supreme knowledge, and a dream was attained.
There was a beautiful image of Kṛṣṇa in front of him, / made of stone, on a golden pedestal, endowed with all auspicious marks.
It was dark as a blue lotus, full of glossy loveliness, / lovely with its threefold bending form, adorned with a peacock feather,
joyfully sounding the golden flute placed upon his lower lip, / and attended by two beautiful women stationed on his right and left,
increasing the desire of both through kisses, embraces, and the like. / Having seen Kṛṣṇa sporting in such attire,
Citradhvaja bowed his head before him, bashful at heart. / Then Hari, smiling, spoke to his beloved who stood on his right side:
“Having created a wonderful divine maiden's form, equal to yourself, / for this bashful and supreme one who has come to our body’s seat,
O deer-eyed one, meditate upon non-difference with your own body; / then, touched by the splendors of your limb, he shall obtain your form.”
Then that lotus-petal-eyed lady, approaching Citradhvaja, / stood meditating upon the non-difference of his limbs with her own limbs.
Then the splendors from her body completely filled his limbs: / from the brilliance of her two breasts, his full and lovely breasts were born;
from the brilliance of her hips, a charming disc of hips was born; / from the brilliance of her locks, a braid of hair arose; from her two hands, two hands [arose].
Thus everything was fully accomplished: ornaments, garments, garlands, and the like; / she became skilled in the arts, with fragrance in her inner self.
Beholding the fortunate maiden on earth, like one lamp from another, / charming with the beauty of a smile that dispels Citradhvaja’s inner shame,
grasping her by both hands with love, she gladly led her away, / and embracing that beloved standing on Govinda’s left side,
she said: “This is your maidservant; bestow a name upon her, / and lovingly assign her service, as agreeable and dear to you.”
Then, according to her own inclination, she gave her the name ‘Citrakalā,’ / and smiling, she held out a lute for the sake of service:
“Always stay nearby, sing with various melodies / of the virtues of the lord of life; this duty is assigned to you.”
Then Citrakalā, taking the command and bowing to Mādhava / and to his beloved’s feet, taking the dust of their feet,
sang a very sweet song that caused joy to them both. / Then she was lovingly embraced by Kṛṣṇa, the embodiment of bliss.
As long as she was filled in the ocean of bliss, just then Citradhvaja / awoke, overcome with great love and absorbed in recollection.
For that very supreme bliss, he wept aloud with an open throat; / weeping from that time onward, speaking only what pertained to Hari,
though addressed by his father and others, he never spoke a word to anyone. / Staying at home for merely a month, taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa at midnight,
he went out and practiced severe asceticism in the forest, difficult for sages to perform. / At the end of the cosmic age, casting off his body through ascetic penance alone, that great sage
became the auspicious daughter of the cowherd named Vīragupta, / named Citrakalā herself, on whose charming shoulder
a lute adorned with the seven notes is always seen. / She stands on the left, holding a wonderful jeweled pitcher,
and in her right hand she holds a jeweled spittoon. / In ancient times, there was a sage greeted by all ascetics,
named Puṇyaśravas, of the Kāśyapa gotra, knowing all duties. / His father was a devotee of Śiva, who daily, with the Śatarudrīya,
praised the god, the lord of gods, the lord of the universe, who is affectionate to his devotees. / Being pleased, the blessed Śaṃkara, along with Pārvatī,
appeared visibly at midnight on the fourteenth day and granted a boon: / “Your son will indeed be a devotee of Kṛṣṇa while still a child.”
Initiate him in his eighth year; give him this perfected mantra, / taught by me, with twenty-one syllables, as I declare to you.
This mantra, named the knowledge of Gopāla, bestows mastery of speech; / on the tip of the tongue of one who practices it, marvelous pastimes appear.
He whose forms are infinite comes of his own accord, bestowing boons. / Splendid with Kāma, Māyā, Ramā, Kaṇṭha, Indra, and Dāmodara,

having uttered the ten-syllable mantra in the middle, one should state those very syllables again. / I will also tell you the seer and so forth, as well as the meditation taught for the ten-syllable mantra.
In the midst of an ocean of full nectar, one should recall an island made of light; / there, in the forest of Vṛndāvana, encircled by the Kālindī, one should meditate.
It is surrounded by trees and creepers dropping flowers in all seasons, / resounding with the calls of dancing, intoxicated peacocks, and the singing of cuckoos and bees.
In the middle of it stands a single great pārijāta tree, / extending with branches and sub-branches, rising a hundred yojanas high.
At its pure base, all around, is a circle of cows; / within that is a circle of cowherd boys holding flutes and horns.
Within that is a charming circle of fair-browed women of Vraja, / bearing various gifts in their hands, their minds overwhelmed with passion;
and a circle of those whose hands are folded in reverence, clad in white garments, / adorned with white ornaments, their inner beings overwhelmed with love.
One should contemplate the daughters of the Śrutis receiving his beloved words. / Then on a jeweled altar one should meditate on Hari covered in fine silk,
lying upon Rādhā’s thigh as if on the stem of a plantain tree, / gazing at her captivating face, which smiles sweetly like the moon,
his left foot slightly bent, with his left hand, flute in grasp, / embracing his beloved, and with his right hand touching her chin,
radiant like a great emerald and having the luster of pearls, / with wide eyes like lotus petals, dressed in spotless yellow garments,
his head shining with a mass of peacock feathers, charming with a necklace of pearls, / adorned with beautiful makara-shaped earrings shining at the edge of his cheeks,
wearing a garland of tulasī down to his feet, adorned with bracelets and armlets, / and encircled by anklets, signet rings, and a girdle.

One should meditate on him as exceedingly delicate, endowed with the age of youth. / The worship is that taught for the ten-syllable mantra, and the preliminary rite requires four hundred thousand [repetitions].
Having spoken thus, the god and the virtuous goddess, the mountain's daughter, vanished; / the sage returned and instructed his son in the very same way.
Puṇyaśravas, indeed, through the mere reception of that mantra, himself described Keśava / with diverse [praises], surpassing all the sages,
in characteristics of form, charm, cleverness, and astonishing beauty. / Then, joyful in mind, the boy departed from his home.
Subsisting on air, he practiced austerities for thirty thousand kalpas. / At the end of that, she herself was born in Gokula, in the house of Nanda's brother,
named Lavaṅgā, watching for Kṛṣṇa's hints, / in whose hand an instrument for cleaning his face is seen.
Thus I have told you of some of the foremost beloveds of Kṛṣṇa.

Whatever person here reads or causes others to read with devotion this chapter, filled with the various aesthetic sentiments of Hari / and with the excellent daughters of Vraja possessed of charming smiles and eyes, goes to the abode of the blessed Lord Vāsudeva.

5.73.m: The Lord said: / That wonder which was asked by you has been spoken by me in order; / where Brahmā and the other gods are bewildered, who indeed would not be bewildered?
Even so, I shall tell you what was spoken by the supreme sage / to the great king Ambarīṣa, the devotee of Viṣṇu accompanied by auspiciousness.
Having reached the hermitage of Badarī, the king, bowing down with a desire to know the dharma of Viṣṇu, / praised the self-controlled one who was seated there,
Vedavyāsa, highly fortunate, all-knowing, the highest of men: / “You ought to protect me here in this insurmountable cycle of worldly existence.
I am detached from sense objects; homage to you, homage completely! / That state which is free from anxiety, whose form is being, consciousness, and bliss,
the supreme Brahman, the supreme space, non-space, free from affliction, / which the sages perceive directly and so cross over the ocean of worldly existence—
how might my mind constantly attain a path toward that?” / Vyāsa said: / “An extremely secret thing has been asked by you, which was not told by me to Śuka,
my own son; but I will speak to you, who are dear to Hari. / This supreme universe was [existent], whatever form it had, where it was established;
listen to that unmanifest, untroubled realm, consisting of the Lord. / Formerly, austerities were performed by me for many thousands of years,
resorting to food consisting of fruits, roots, leaves, water, and air. / Then the blessed Lord Hari spoke to me, engaged in meditating upon him:
‘For what purpose is your desire to act, or what is your desire to know, O highly intelligent one? / I am pleased; choose a boon from the best of boon-givers.
Seeing me brings an end to worldly existence; this truth I speak to you.’ / Then I spoke to Kṛṣṇa, my body bristling with horripilation:
‘I wish to see you with both eyes, O Madhusūdana! / That true, supreme Brahman, light of the world, lord of the world,
which the crowns of the Vedas declare—that wondrous lord visible to the eyes.’ / The blessed Lord said: / ‘Just as formerly I was asked and petitioned in this manner by Brahmā,
what I spoke to him, that is told to you as well. / Some call me Prakṛti, and likewise Puruṣa, and the Lord;
some call me dharma, some wealth, some liberation, free from fear; / some call me the void, some being, some Śiva, some Sadāśiva.
Others call me the one eternal one abiding in the crown of the Vedas, / true existence, devoid of change, whose form is being, consciousness, and bliss.
Behold now: I will reveal my own form, hidden in the Vedas.’ / Then, O king, I saw a child, radiant as a dark rain cloud,
surrounded by cowherd maidens, a cowherd laughing with the cowherd boys, / seated at the base of a kadamba tree, wearing yellow garments, wondrous.
I saw the forest named Vṛndāvana, adorned with fresh sprouts, / filled with the sounds of cuckoos and black bees, captivating as the god of love.
I saw the river Kālindī, having the luster of blue lotus petals; / then I saw Govardhana, held up by the hand of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma,
for the destruction of the pride of great Indra, bringing delight to cows and cowherds; / and Gopāla, accompanied by women, joyful, playing the flute.
Having seen him, the ornament of all ornaments, I became exceedingly rejoiced. / Then the blessed Lord, who roams Vṛndāvana, himself said to me:
‘This divine, eternal form of mine which has been seen by you, / partless, actionless, tranquil, whose form is being, consciousness, and bliss,
complete, with eyes like lotus petals, nothing is higher than this of mine. / These very Vedas call this the cause of causes,
the true, eternal, supreme bliss, dense consciousness, everlasting, auspicious. / Know my Mathurā to be eternal, and likewise the forest of Vṛndāvana,
the Yamunā, the cowherd girls, and likewise the cowherd boys. / This descent of mine is eternal; have no doubt about this.
Rādhā is indeed always cherished by me; I am all-knowing, higher than the highest, / possessing all desires, lord of all, all-blissful, higher than the highest.
In me this entire universe shines forth, unfolded by illusion.’ / Then I spoke to the god, the cause of the causes of the world:
‘Who are the cowherd maidens, and who are the cowherds? What is this tree considered to be? / What is the forest, and what are the cuckoos and the rest? What is this river, and what is the mountain?’

And who is that fortunate flute, the sole vessel of joy for the worlds?
Pleased, with a gracious lotus face, the Blessed One said to me:

“The cowherd women are to be known as the Vedic hymns, and the cowherd maidens are the verses of the Ṛgveda;
and the daughters of the gods, O king of kings, are seekers of liberation endowed with ascetic austerity.

All the cowherds are sages, the embodiments of Vaikuṇṭha’s bliss;
this kadamba tree is a wish-fulfilling tree, the sole vessel of supreme bliss.

The forest is named Ānandaka, destroying heinous sins;
and the cuckoos and other birds are the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Gandharvas, without a doubt.

Some consider the Yamunā’s form to be the very heart of bliss itself;
this mountain is the beginningless servant of Hari, of this there is no doubt.

Hear about the flute, that brāhmaṇa, so that it may be known to you as well.
There was a brāhmaṇa of tranquil mind, dedicated to asceticism and tranquility,

named Devavrata, self-controlled, skilled in the ritual section [of the Vedas];
he lived in the midst of a multitude of Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to religious rites.

O lord of the earth, he once heard: ‘There is a Lord of sacrifice!’
Then a brāhmaṇa whose resolution was fixed on me arrived at his house.

That devotee of mine performed worship somewhere with tulasī leaves and water;
he offered some fruit and roots in that [householder’s] home.

The wise brāhmaṇa intentionally gave him some bathwater and fruit;
smiling without faith, he too accepted them from the brāhmaṇa.

By that sin arose the exceedingly terrible state of being a flute;
by that merit, however, he attained the state of being dear to me.

Along with me, O king of kings, he shines like a banner;
at the end of the cosmic age, having become devoted to Viṣṇu, he will attain Brahman.

Ah, evil-minded men do not know my eternal, supreme city,
that ancient, charming Mathurā praised by the kings of gods, serpents, and sages!

Although there are cities such as Kāśī, Mathurā alone is blessed among them,
for it confers liberation upon men in four ways: by birth, by the initiation with the muñjā belt, by death, and by cremation.

Only when people are purified through asceticism and the like, with auspicious thoughts, constantly possessing meditation as their wealth,
do they see my supreme city, O best of brāhmaṇas, and not otherwise even in hundreds of cosmic ages.

The residents of Mathurā are blessed, venerable even to the gods;
their majesty is immeasurable, and all of them are four-armed.

Those men who look for faults in the residents of Mathurā
do not see their own fault born of a thousand births and deaths.

Even if destitute, those who remember Mathurā are blessed,
where the god Bhūteśvara grants liberation even to sinners.

The supreme god Bhūteśvara is eternally most dear to me;
out of love for me, he never abandons that city.

A person of bad conduct who does not bow to Bhūteśvara, worship him, or remember him
would never see this Mathurā of mine, which is self-luminous and called the Supreme Deity.

How can that sinful man attain devotion to me
who does not worship Śiva, my supreme devotee?

Those lowest of men, whose minds are mostly deluded by my māyā,
do not bow to Bhūteśvara, nor do they remember or praise him.

Where even the boy Dhruva, devoted to my worship,
attained the supreme, pure station sought with effort by the ancestors.

Having reached that city of Mathurā, mine and difficult even for gods to attain,
one should cast off one’s very life-breaths, even if lame or blind.

O highly fortunate Vedavyāsa, do not harbour any doubt anywhere;
this secret of the crown of the Vedas has been revealed to you by me.”

Whoever, being pure, recites this chapter spoken by the Blessed One,
or whoever hears it with devotion, attains eternal liberation.

5.74.m:
The Lord said:
Once in secret, the glorious Uddhava, the beloved attendant of the Lord,
asked Sanatkumāra in solitude, O Lord:

“Where Govinda sports eternally with the cowherd maidens
in that eternal abode of the gods, where is that supreme place, or what is it like?

The accounts of those various pastimes and whatever else is wonderful—
if that is known to you, it must be told, if affection for me exists.”

Sanatkumāra said:
“Once, on the bank of the Yamunā beneath a certain tree,
as the attendant of the Lord, endowed with good conduct, was seated,

that secret experience of his, and whatever was seen and done
even by the great-souled son of Pṛthā, was recounted to me in conversation.

That I shall tell you; listen with supreme attentiveness;
however, this must never be disclosed anywhere at any time.”

Arjuna said:
“O ocean of mercy, that which has not been seen or heard by Śaṅkara, Viriñci, and the others—
all this, O Lord, tell out of compassion!

Was it not told by you previously that the cowherd women are your beloveds?
Of how many kinds are they, O Lord, or how many are they in number?

How many are their names, who are they, and where do they dwell?
How many are their duties, and what are their age and dress, O Lord?

With whom and where will you sport in secret, O God,
in eternal, everlasting joy, and in eternal splendour, in forest after forest?

What is that place like, and where is that eternal, supreme, great place?
If there is such compassion [in you], then you ought to tell me all this here.

Whatever was unasked even by me, and whatever secret of yours is unknown,
O dispeller of the distress of the afflicted, O fortunate one, you will tell all of that.”

The Blessed One said:
“Truly, that place, those beloveds of mine, and that pastime of mine
are inaccessible even to men who are as dear as life.

If it is spoken, an intense longing to see it will arise in you, my child;
that which is invisible to Brahmā and the others—what [to speak of it] to any other person?

Therefore desist, my child! What would please you without this?”
Having heard this exceedingly harsh speech of the Blessed One,
Humble, Arjuna fell like a staff at his pair of lotus feet; / then the all-pervading Lord smiled and lifted him up with both arms.

and said with supreme love to his devotee, as he is affectionate to his devotees:
“Then what is the use of telling it here, since it must indeed be seen by you?

Having worshipped with supreme devotion the glorious goddess Tripurasundarī,
in whom everything has arisen, in whom it still abides today, and into whom it will dissolve,

surrender yourself to her;
without her, I am never able to bestow this realm.”

Having heard this word of the Blessed One, the son of Pṛthā, his eyes filled with joy,
went to the place of the glorious sandals of the glorious goddess Tripurā.

Having gone there, he saw this glorious alter of wish-fulfilling gems,
exceedingly adorned with stairs fashioned out of various jewels.

There [he saw] a wish-fulfilling tree, bowed down with various flowers and fruits,
with tender leaves of all seasons dripping with drops of sweet nectar,

made radiant by shoots waving in the wind as if raining down,
resounding with parrots, flocks of cuckoos, mynas, pigeons,

playful cakora birds, and charming birds,
filled with the humming commotion of royal bees.

Beneath it stood a most wonderful, divine temple of glorious gems,
charming with glittering jewels like a rising forest fire.

There stood a jewel-throne, exceedingly captivating with great golden radiance;
upon it [he saw] her, resembling the morning sun, adorned with various ornaments,

endowed with fresh youth, her creeper-like four arms shining
with goad, noose, bow, and arrows, very gracious, and enchanting,

her lotus feet illuminated by the jewel-rays from the crowns of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others,
surrounded by the supernatural powers of Aṇimā and the rest;

the goddess of smiling countenance, who grants boons and is fond of her devotees.
Having made himself known, saying, 'I am Arjuna,' and bowing down again and again,

standing alone with folded hands, filled with an abundance of devotion,
she, a treasury of mercy, knowing his worship, granted her favor.

Overwhelmed by the remembrance of him, the goddess spoke out of compassion.
The blessed Goddess said:
'What rare gift was given by you, dear child, to a worthy recipient?

What sacrifice was offered here, or what austerity was performed?
Or what spotless devotion to the Lord was acquired by you previously?

Or what rare [virtue], what great auspicious deed [was done] in this world,
by which such grace has been granted with joy by the Lord to you who took refuge?

A grace most deeply hidden and unattainable by anyone else has been bestowed by the Lord.
There is nothing like this for mortals, nor for dwellers on the earth,

nor for dwellers in heaven, gods and others, nor for ascetics, lords, and yogins,
nor indeed for all devotees—never, never, and never at all!

Yet grace was bestowed upon you, child, as by the Soul of the universe.
Therefore, come, and having understood, worship at the Kulakuṇḍa, my lake.

This goddess grants all desires; go together with her.
Bathe there according to the rules and quickly return here.'

Having gone there at that very moment and bathed, Pārtha returned as directed.
When he had returned, having performed his bath, the nyāsa, mudrās, offerings, and the rest,

having been caused to be performed, the supreme vidyā of Bālā,
which yields immediate siddhi, was then spoken by the goddess into his right ear:

the second [vidyā], adorned by the universe, beyond the half of the syllable *ha*.
And the practice, the worship, and recitation numbering one hundred thousand,

and the application properly performed with oleander buds—
having had all this carried out, the supreme Mistress said this to him out of compassion:

'By this very method let my worship be performed.
Then, when I am pleased, for the sake of bestowing grace upon you,

you shall then have the entitlement to enter those [innermost] precincts.
This was the rule established previously by the Lord himself.'

Having heard this, Arjuna worshipped her with that armour;
then, having performed the worship and recitation, the goddess was pleased.

Then, having performed the auspicious homa and bath according to the rule,
considering himself as one who had achieved his purpose, having almost fulfilled his desire,

Pārtha thought all spiritual perfection to be in the palm of his hand.
At that moment, the goddess approached him with a smiling face

and said: 'Go now, dear child, into the inner chamber of that mansion.'
Then, thrilled with excitement, Pārtha stood up full of joy,

his heart filled with boundless joy, and bowed down to her like a stick.
Commanded by her, Arjuna, accompanied by the goddess's female companion,

went to the abode of Rādhā's Lord, which is beyond the reach even of the Siddhas.
And then, having been directed, [to that realm] situated above Goloka,

unmoving, supported by the wind, eternal, true, the abode of all happiness,
named the eternal Vṛndāvana, where the great festival of the eternal Rāsa dance takes place,

he beheld the supreme secret, the essence of the nectar of complete love.
Indeed, at her mere word, beholding that secret with his eyes,

overcome and bewildered by burgeoning love, he fell down there.
Then, regaining consciousness with difficulty, raised up by her with her arms,

and having somehow attained composure through her soothing words,
[he asked:] 'Tell me, what other austerity remains to be performed by me?'
Thus he became restless under the weight of longing to see him; / then, taking her by his hand at that right foot,

reached an auspicious spot, and having arrived, spoke these words:
'For bathing, enter this expanse of auspicious water, O Pārtha,

the central bud of a formation situated in a thousand-petalled lotus,
with four lakes, four streams, filled with an abundance of marvels.

Entering inside it, you will see a wonder here.
To the southern part of this, here is a lake

which is the drinking of honey and mead, named the Malaya Stream;
and this is the blossoming garden where in the spring the festival of love

Govinda celebrates, suitable for spring blossoms,
where they praise Kṛṣṇa's incarnation day and night,

and by whose mere remembrance a sprout of love arises in the sage's heart.
Therefore, having bathed in this lake and gone to the bank of the eastern lake,

sip its water and attain your desired purpose.'
Then, having heard her words, into the water of that lake,

which was tinged with pollen fallen from white water-lilies, night-blooming lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses,
and charmingly scented with drops of honey,

swaying with the sounds of royal swans and other birds on its broad banks,
with its four shores paved with jewels, rippled by gentle breezes—

when Pārtha had plunged into the water, she vanished right there.
Rising up and looking around, bewildered, sweetly smiling,

with a slender creeper-like body fair and radiant as the rays of freshly purified gold,
in the prime of her blooming youth, her face resembling the autumn moon,

with glossy, deep-blue, curling locks of hair adorned with glistening gems,
her forehead band resplendent with the radiance of a sindūra mark,

the playful movement of whose unfolding creeper-like brows surpassed the bow of love,
with wagtail-like eyes playfully darting and flashing, deep and dark,

the orbs of whose cheeks were gleaming with the radiant light of jeweled earrings,
with splendid, wondrous creeper-like arms tender as lotus stalks,

her sprout-like hands stealing all the beauty of autumn lotuses,
with an inner garment held by a girdle of gold crafted by a skilled artisan,

her hips radiant with the ends of a jingling zone of bells,
her rounded hips and thighs, an abode of beauty, enveloped in shining silken cloth,

her lovely lotus feet adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets,
possessing skill in the various arts of glowing passion,

endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament,
she looked upon herself as a wondrous, foremost maiden.

And through the illusory power of the Lord of the cowherd maidens' lives,
she completely forgot whatever belonged to her previous body immediately after that.
Bewildered as to what to do, she stood there in great wonder; / in the meantime, a deep, sudden sound arose in the sky.

'O fair-browed one, go by this very path to the eastern lake;
sip its water and fulfill your cherished desire.

For your female companions are there, do not despair, O fair-complexioned one!
They will indeed bestow your desired boon right there.'
Hearing this divine voice, she went to the eastern lake, / which had diverse ancient streams and was filled with various birds,
shining with blooming white water-lilies, red lotuses, blue water-lilies, and others, / with rubies, and its fine banks with lotus steps.

its four shores adorned with charming bowers, creepers, and trees abounding in various blossoms;
she sipped the water and stood for a moment.

Just then, into the hollow of her attentive ears, she heard the tinkling of small bells,
accompanied by the jingling of a resonant girdle and charming anklets.

And then [she saw] a band of beautiful women, endowed with wondrous youth,
with wondrous ornaments in place, and wondrous appearance and speech.
Having wonderful limbs, unprecedented, she [possessed] distinct wondrous charms, / wonderful speech, wonderful laughter, glances, and the like,
charming, wonderful beauty, endowed with all sweetness, / reaching an endless realm of pure beauty, captivatingly and delightfully fair,
endowed with wondrous tender loveliness, wondrous grace and favors, / a gathering of all wonders, wondrous in glances and the rest.
Having seen that supreme wonder, pondering somewhat in her heart, / drawing on the earth with her big toe, she stood with a bowed face.
Then there was agitation among them, and mutual glances: / “Who is this of our own kind, long an object of boundless curiosity?”
Seeing all of them, [saying,] 'She should be known,' for a moment / those skilled in counsel invited [them] and, out of curiosity, came to see.
Having come, one among them, renowned by the name Priyamudā, / a wise woman, with sweet speech lovingly spoke to her:
Priyamudā said: / “Who are you? Whose daughter are you? Whose beloved are you? / Where were you born? By whom were you brought here, or did you come yourself?
Tell all this to us; what use is anxiety? / In this place of supreme bliss, can anyone have sorrow?”
Questioned thus by her, she bowed down in humility / and spoke in a sweet voice, charming their minds:
Arjuna said: / “Who I am, whose daughter I am, or where born, whose beloved, / or by whom brought here, or whether I came myself—
I know none of this; may the noble lady know it yet. / Listen to that which I tell, if you have faith in my word:
On the very southern side of this place there is a lake; / I came there to bathe, and there I remained.
Filled with deep longing, then looking around in all directions, / I heard a wonderful sound arisen from the sky:

'O fair-browed one, go by this very path to the eastern lake;
sip its water and fulfill your cherished desire.
For there are your friends, O woman of excellent complexion, do not despond! / For they will bring about your desired boon right there!’
Hearing his words, she came here from there, / her heart filled with dejection and joy, overwhelmed with anxiety.
Having come and touched its water, I heard various auspicious sounds, / and after that I saw your supreme ladyships.
This much alone I know in body, mind, and speech; / this very thing has been told by me, O goddesses, if it pleases you.
Who are you? Whose daughters? Where born? Whose beloveds?” / Having heard that speech of hers, that Priyamudā indeed spoke:
“Let it be so: we are the life-friends of that very [Lord], O auspicious one, / maiden-companions in sport with the moon of Vṛndāvana, happily [dwelling here].
Delighting in the Self with him, those maidens of Vraja have come here; / these are known as the multitudes of Vedic texts, and these likewise as the sages.
We are indeed cowherd maidens, told to you in our true nature. / Here, born from the body of Rādhā's lord, are the foremost dearest ones,
eternal, eternal sporting maidens, roaming the grounds of eternal play. / This goddess is Pūrṇarasā, and this is Rasamantharā;
this is named Rasālayā, and this is Rasavallarī; / this is Rasapīyūṣadhārā, this is Rasataraṅgiṇī;
and this is Rasakallolinī, and this is Rasavāpikā; / this very one is Anaṅgasenā, and this is Anaṅgamālinī;
this maiden is Madayantī, and this is Rasavihvalā; / and this is named Lalitā, and this is Lalitayauvanā;
and this is Anaṅgakusumā, this is Madanamañjarī; / this is named Kalāvatī, this is remembered as Ratikalā;
this is named Kāmakalā, this is indeed Kāmadāyinī; / this maiden is Ratilolā, this maiden is Ratotsukā;
and this is Ratisarvasvā, but that one is Raticintāmaṇi. / Certain ones among these are Nityānandās, grantors of the flavor of eternal love.
Next are the groups of Vedic texts; listen to some of them here: / This is Udgītā, this is Sugītā, and this beloved is Kalagītā;
this is known as Kalasvarā; this maiden is Kalakaṇṭhikā; / this is Vipañcī, this is Kramapadā, this is considered Bahuhutā;
this is Bahuprayogā; this young woman is known as Bahukalā; / this is known as Kalāvatī, and this is considered Kriyāvatī.
Next are the groups of sages; here are some of them: / This is named Ugratapā, this is remembered as Bahuguṇā;
this is named Priyavratā, and this is considered Suvratā; / this maiden is considered Surekhā; this is Suparvā, bestowing much;
this is known as Ratnarekhā, and that one is considered Maṇigrīvā; / and this is Suparṇā, this is Ākalpā, Sukalpā, Ratnamālikā;
this is Saudāminī, a fair-browed woman, and this is Kāmadāyinī; / and this is known as Bhogadā; this chaste one is considered Viśvā;
and this is Dhāriṇī, Dhātrī, Sumedhā, and that one Kānti; / this is Aparṇā, this is Suparṇā, and this is considered Sulakṣaṇā;
this is Sudatī, and this is Guṇavatī, that one is considered Sukalinī; / this is known as Sulocanā, and this is remembered as Sumanas;
and Aśrutā, and Suśīlā, who bestows the happiness of love. / Hereafter are the cowherd maidens, we who have come here;
may some of them be recognized, O lotus-faced one: / That one is Candrāvalī, and this is Candrikā, considered auspicious;
this is Candrāvalī, this is Candrarekhā, and that one is Candrikā; / this is known as Candramālā, and this is considered Candrālikā;
this is Candraprabhā; this young woman is remembered as Candrakalā; / this is Varṇāvalī, this is Varṇamālā, this is Maṇimālikā;
this is celebrated as Varṇaprabhā, this is Suprabhā, this Maṇiprabhā; / this is Hārāvalī, this is Tārāmālinī, considered auspicious;
this is Mālatī, this is Yūthī, Vāsantī, Navamallikā; / this is Mallī, this is Navamallī, that one is considered Śephālikā;
this is Sauganthikā, Kastūrī, this is Padminī, Kumudvatī; / this very one is Rasollāsā, and this is Citravṛndasamā;
this is Rambhā, and this is Urvaśī, Surekhā, Svarṇarekhikā; / this is Kāñcanamālā, and this other is Satyasantatikā.
All these have been introduced; others are also to be recognized. / Accompanied by these, along with us, you will sport, O passionate lady!
Come to the shore of the eastern lake; having bathed you there / in accordance with the rules, O friend, I will then impart the mantra that brings realization.”
Having quickly brought her thus and bathed her according to the rules, / with the supreme mantra of the beloved of the lord of arts of Vṛndāvana,
she made her receive in brief, preceded by the initiation rites: / higher than the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, placed after the seed-syllable of Agni,
joined with the fourth vowel, adorned with nāda and bindu, / enclosed by two praṇavas, and exceedingly rare in the three worlds.
By the mere reception of the mantra, all realization comes to pass. / The rule for preparatory rites, meditation, the count of fire-offerings and muttering [were taught]:
[Meditation upon] the one whose limbs are fair as molten gold, adorned with various ornaments, / of wondrous form and beauty, gracious, granting boons,
with kalhāra flowers, karavīra and other flowers, campakas, lotuses, / and other fragrant flowers along with saugandhika lilies,
and with water for washing the feet, respectful offerings, sipping-water, enchanting incenses and lamps, / and various divine food-offerings joyfully brought by the host of female companions.
Having duly worshipped the goddess, recited one hundred thousand mantras, / sacrificed in accordance with the rules, praised her, and bowed like a stick upon the earth,
then that praised goddess, unblinking within, / having fashioned her own shadow by her power of illusion, according to her own desire,
and then stationing that beloved at her side as if by force, / surrounded by her female companions, delighted by the pure acts of worship, recitation, and so on,
and by the hymns of praise, devotion, and prostrations, she then appeared out of compassion, / shining with the hue of golden campaka flowers, resplendent with diverse ornaments,
her form charming with grace and beauty in every major and minor limb, / her auspicious face like the spotless full autumn moon,
enchanting the three worlds with her gentle, charming smile and gaze, / completely illuminating the ten directions with her own radiance.
Then that goddess, granting boons and affectionate toward her devotees, spoke. / The goddess said: 'The word of my companions is true; therefore, you are my dear friend.
Arise! Come! I shall fulfill your desire.' / And having heard that word of the goddess, which was her own cherished desire,
Arjunī, her limbs charming with horripilation, her eyes filled with tears, / and overcome with love, fell once again at the goddess's feet.
Then she said to Priyaṃvadā, the goddess [spoke] to this companion: / 'Taking [her] by the hand, comforting her, bring her along with me.'
Then Priyaṃvadā, eager by the command of the goddess, / taking her along in that very manner, went in the company of the goddess.
Having gone to the northern shore of the lake and bathed her according to rule, / having performed the preliminary rites beginning with the declaration of intention and worshipped properly,
the goddess, beloved of Hari, graciously made her receive / that mantra of the glorious Lord of the arts of Gokula, which grants complete success.
The observance named Gokulanātha, adorned of old by Mohana, / a mantra bestowing all accomplishments, kept secret in all the Tantras,
she, understanding its significance, gave her unwavering devotion to Govinda; / and the meditation upon Him was told, and this king of mantras, the enchanting one,
taught in the Mohana Tantra, the mere memory of which grants success: / 'Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, adorned with various ornaments,
having the beauty of ten million Kāmadevas, immersed in the aesthetic rapture of the rāsa-dance, one should meditate upon Him.' / Desiring to purify her, she spoke this secret to Priyaṃvadā:
The glorious Rādhikā said: / 'Until her excellent preliminary observance is complete, / you, being attentive together with the female companions, must protect her.'
Having spoken thus, she went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet, / leaving behind a shadow born of herself for her beloveds.
Rādhikā, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, stood there just as before. / There, by the instruction of Priyaṃvadā, an auspicious eight-petaled lotus
was fashioned with gorocanā, saffron, and sandalwoods, / [drawn] with these various substances mixed together, bestowing success.
Having inscribed the king of yantras and that pure, wondrous mantra, / having performed the preliminary placement of mantras and the rest, and water for the feet and guest-water according to rule,
with flowers born of various seasons, with saffron and sandalwoods, / with incenses, lamps, food offerings, betel leaves, and mouth perfumes,
and with garments, ornaments, and garlands, having worshipped the delight of Nanda / along with all his retinue, equipped with weapons and with mounts,
having praised and bowed according to rule, she engaged her mind in recollection. / Then the lord, the son of Yaśodā, subservient to devotion,
his gestures rippling with side-glances accompanied by smiles, / said to the goddess Rādhikā: 'Quickly bring her here.'
Thus commanded, that very goddess, having dispatched the companion Śāradā, / swiftly brought her before the soul of the rāsa-dance.
Approaching the presence of the glorious Kṛṣṇa, overcome with love, / she fell onto the golden ground, beholding everything wonderful.
Having risen with difficulty, slowly opening her eyes, / being overwhelmed by the burden of emotions, with perspiration, horripilation, and trembling,
she first saw a wonderful, enchanting place there; / and then the wish-fulfilling tree there, with glistening emerald leaves,
endowed with sprouts of coral, tender, with a golden trunk, / with roots of crystal and coral, granting the fulfillment of desires and riches,
granting the desired fruit to supplicants; beneath it, a jewel-palace, / a jewel-throne there, and upon it an eight-petaled lotus;
the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, situated to the right and left, / and in the four directions, in their proper places, the wish-fulfilling cows.
All around was the Nandana garden, served by the Malaya breeze, / and by the enchanting fragrances of flowers
of all seasons, everything was perfumed, surpassing dark agallochum; / cooled by a shower of pollen particles, exceedingly charming,
with its interior constantly resounding with the swarms of humming / female bees intoxicated by savoring the nectar,
resounding with the sweet calls of pigeons, male and female cuckoos, / female starlings and parrots, and other beloved birds;
thronged with the dances of intoxicated peacocks, heightening desire; / [she saw Kṛṣṇa,] the luster of whose body was like dark collyrium sprinkled with nectar-water,
whose glossy, black, curling locks were scented with reddish perfume, / the crest of his hair bound with the plumage of an intoxicated peacock and other birds,
with an ear-ornament of flowers on his left ear attended by bees, / illuminated by his mirror-like cheeks shining with moving locks of hair,
resplendent with the beauty of his forehead adorned with an extraordinary tilaka, / whose charming nose was like a sesame flower or the beak of the king of birds,
with charming bimba-fruit lips, awakening Kāmadeva with his gentle smile, / enchanting with a necklace resembling wild flowers,
whose two lovely, plump shoulders shone with a garland of celestial trees / served by thousands of intoxicated, hovering female bees,
his chest gleaming with a pearl necklace and adorned with the Kaustubha jewel, / marked with the Śrīvatsa sign, charming with arms extending to his knees,
with a deep navel, exceptionally handsome with a waist like that of a lion, / charming with thighs like well-grown, shapely trees and shapely knees,
adorned with bracelets, armlets, anklets, and other supreme ornaments, / the master of the shapely hips encircled by yellow silk garments,
surpassing ten million Kāmadevas through his charm and beauty, / with charming musical modes and songs played on the flute,
enchanting and immersing the three worlds in an ocean of joy, / displaying the onset of love in every limb, languid with the rapture of the rāsa-dance;
[she saw him attended by maidens] respectfully holding fly-whisks, fans, garlands, perfumes, sandalwood, / betel, mirrors, drinking vessels, vessels for chewed spices,
and whatever other items belonged to amusement, each individually, / and various charming instruments of music,
stationed in their appropriate places, watching his gestures, / their trembling eyes fixed one by one upon his lotus-face;
and [attended] on the left side by the glorious goddess Rādhikā with reverence, / worshipping him, offering him betel, smiling purely.
Beholding this, Arjunī was overwhelmed by the onset of passion. / Then, knowing her to be in that state, Hṛṣīkeśa, the omniscient,
taking her by the hand in the interior of the grove of all sports, / the all-pervading lord of great yogins, sported in secret as he pleased.
Then, having placed his sprout-like arm upon her shoulder, / he approached and said to Śāradā: 'In this western lake,'
"Quickly bathe this slender-limbed woman, who is tired from sport and softly smiling." / Then goddess Śāradā, in that lake of pastimes,
said to her, "Take a bath!" And weary as she was, she did so. / Entering into the water, she became Arjuna once again.
He emerged where the Lord of the gods, the glorious master of Vaikuṇṭha, was. / Seeing that Arjuna dejected, his mind shattered,
Kṛṣṇa touched him with his hand by his illusory power and restored him to his natural state. / The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: "O Dhanañjaya, I cherish you; you are my dear friend.
There is no one equal to you in the three worlds who knows the secret. / The secret about which you asked has now been experienced by you.
If you speak of it to anyone, Arjuna, then you are bound by an oath to me!" / Sanatkumāra said: Having thus received his favor, his resolve sealed by oaths,
he departed with a joyful heart from that place to his own abode, recollecting the wonder. / Thus everything that was within the range of my knowledge has been told to you,
and likewise there is Govinda's oath to you regarding the telling of it to another." / Īśvara said: Having heard his words, the son of Upagu attained perfection and departed.
He went to Vṛndāvana, the dwelling of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. / Even today he resides there, knowing the eternal sports and pastimes of Kṛṣṇa.
Even when questioned by Nārada, I did not reveal that secret; / yet he attained it after assuming female form.
The secret which I revealed to you out of affection, / that, O auspicious lady, must not be disclosed to anyone, just as your own womb.
Whoever reads or even listens to this wondrous chapter on the greatness of the Lord's devotee / finds delight in Hari.

5.75.m: Pārvatī said: / The secret of Vṛndāvana has been told by you in many ways, O lord. / By what special merit did Nārada attain female form?
Īśvara said: / Long ago, this wondrous account was inquired into by me. / It was the secret spoken by Brahmā, which he had heard from the lotus-mouth of Kṛṣṇa.
Nārada questioned me; then I received this [knowledge]. / "I am not able to speak of that glorification in any way.
What shall I do? Remembering his oath, my mind is depressed." / When, hearing these words of mine, he became dejected,
then, having summoned Brahmā, I commanded him, my dear: / "Tell Nārada that which was spoken by you to me."
Then Brahmā, having heard my words, went together with Nārada / into the presence of Kṛṣṇa, bowed, and asked that very thing.
Brahmā said: / "What is this forest of thirty-two woods, Vṛndāraṇya, O lord of the people? / I wish to hear, O Blessed One; tell me if I am worthy."
The Blessed One said: / "This charming Vṛndāvana is purely my own abode, / where the beasts, trees, insects, humans, and immortals are directly mine.
Those who live close to me, when dead, come into my presence. / And the wives of the cowherds who dwell here in my abode,
they are indeed yoginīs devoted to me, my deities. / This forest of five yojanas is indeed of divine form.
This Kālindī river is named Suṣumnā, carrying the supreme nectar, / where gods and spirits abide in subtle form.
I am all-pervading and I shall never abandon the forest anywhere. / Appearance and disappearance occur here age after age.
This place is full of light, invisible to the eyes of the flesh. / Behold my secret and my majesty, Vṛndāvana in this age.
It cannot be seen in any way by the deities beginning with Brahmā." / Īśvara said: Having heard that, Nārada bowed to Kṛṣṇa and to Brahmā,
and came to the earthly world, to the sacred forest of Naimiṣa. / There he was honored by Śaunaka and the other chief sages,
and questioned: "O holy one, where have you come from now? Tell us!" / Hearing that, Nārada said: "I have come from Goloka,
having heard the secret of Vṛndāvana from the lotus-mouth of Kṛṣṇa." / Nārada said: "Various kinds of questions were asked there again and again.
All the mantras and the yogas were heard by me there; / I shall recount those very things according to the question, in truth."
Śaunaka and the others said: / "Explain to us the secret of Vṛndāraṇya which was spoken to you by Brahmā, / if you have compassion for us."
Nārada said: / Once on the bank of the Sarayū Gautama was seen by us, / wise, yet deeply sorrowful, his mind agitated by worry.
Seeing me, divine Gautama fell to the surface of the earth. / I myself said to him: "Rise, child, my child!
Why are you so pensive? Speak, if it pleases you." / Gautama said: "From your mouth alone was the reality of Kṛṣṇa heard as it is,
and the secret known as Dvārakā and that known as Mathurā repeatedly by me; / but the secret of Vṛndāvana has not been heard from your lotus-mouth,
by which steadfastness of my mind will come to be, O true guru!" / Nārada said: "This is indeed the supreme mystery, the secret beyond secrets,
pertaining to Vṛndāvana, as was told to me long ago by Brahmā. / [I had said,] 'O lord of the gods, O father, tell me the secret of Vṛndāraṇya!'
Hearing what was inquired, he became silent for a moment; / then [he said]: 'Do not [worry], O child; go to Mahāviṣṇu, my master.'
I too must go there along with you, without a doubt.' / Having spoken thus and taken me along, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
And that very thing which had been stated by me was told to Mahāviṣṇu. / Hearing that, Mahāviṣṇu then commanded the Self-born Brahmā:
'By my command, take the sage Nārada / and direct him to bathe in the lake called Amṛtasaras.'
Commanded by Mahāviṣṇu, the Self-born did so with me. / There I entered the lake of nectar and performed my bath.
Instantly, on the other bank of that lake, I was in the presence of women, / endowed with all auspicious marks, transformed into a woman, thoroughly astonished.
Seeing me approach, they questioned me repeatedly. / The women said: / 'Who are you? From where have you come? Tell of your doings!'
Hearing their affectionate speech, listen to what was said by me: / 'From where? Who am I that have arrived? Or how do I have the form of a woman?
Everything appears like a dream, or am I deluded on the earth?' / Hearing these words of mine, a goddess spoke in sweet tones:
'This city is named Vṛndā, ever dear to moon-like Kṛṣṇa; / and I am goddess Lalitā, beyond the fourth state and devoid of parts.'
Having said this, the great goddess, her mind dense with compassion, / said to me again: 'O goddess, come along with me.'
And all the other women, devoted to Kṛṣṇa's feet, / also said to me in this way: 'Come along with her!'
Then, out of grace, the fourteen-syllabled mantra of moon-like Kṛṣṇa / was spoken by that great-souled goddess.
From that very moment I attained resemblance to them, having various likenesses. / Together with them, I went to where eternal Kṛṣṇa was,
who is pure existence, consciousness, and bliss, the Lord Himself filled with female nature. / His heart filled with the bliss of women, seeing me, he spoke repeatedly:
"Come, beloved lover! Embrace me with devotion!" / And there, O best of the twice-born, he took delight with me for the span of a year.
Then it was said by the Lord of lovers to the goddess Rādhikā: / "This was my prakṛti there, bearing the form of Nārada.
Having led [her] to the delightful nectar lake, direct [her] to bathe." / After that, sweet words were spoken to me by my lover:
"I am the goddess Lalitā, and I am celebrated as Rādhikā; / and I am named Vāsudeva, constantly composed of the arts of love.
Truly, I am female in my essential nature, and I am the eternal female; / and I am the goddess Lalitā who has taken male form as the body of Kṛṣṇa.
There is no difference between us two; truly, truly indeed, O Nārada! / The one who thus knows my reality, the ritual observance, and the mantra,
the proper conduct, and the secret sign, is dear to me like Lalitā. / This [place] named Vṛndāvana is my secret home.
It must never be revealed anywhere, nor ever spoken to a beast." / Thereupon the goddess Rādhikā, having led me to that lake,
stood [there], and then went back to the feet of the moon-like Kṛṣṇa. / Then, solely from plunging into [the water], I returned as Nārada.
With vīṇā in hand, devoted to singing that secret over and over with joy, / having bowed to the Self-born [Brahmā], I went there as an attendant of Viṣṇu.
It was seen as such by the Self-born, and nothing further was spoken then. / Thus, my child, this most secret matter has been told to you by me.
You also must conceal with great effort this realm of the moon-like Kṛṣṇa, which is pure consciousness and art, / just as a mother's paramour [is kept secret], O dear one.
Just as it was spoken by me to my disciple Gautama with its secrets, / so it has been told to you all in its entirety, and it is most concealed.
If it is ever revealed anywhere, O foremost among sages, / then the curse of the moon-like Kṛṣṇa will surely fall, O brāhmaṇas!
Whoever reads or even hears this excellent chapter, / endowed with the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa, attains the supreme abode.

5.76.m: The Lord said: Hearing that Śiśupāla had been slain here, Dantavaktra came to Mathurā to fight with Kṛṣṇa.

Hearing that, Kṛṣṇa mounted his chariot and came with him to Mathurā.

Then, having slain him, crossed the Yamunā, and gone to the cowherd station of Nanda, he greeted his parents, comforted them, and was embraced by them.
the elder cowherds, embraced them, comforted them, he gratified all those who lived there with many garments, ornaments, and the like.
On the delightful bank of the Yamunā, crowded with sacred trees, he lived there for three nights in the joy of sport with the cowherd women day and night.

All the people living there, beginning with the cowherd Nanda, together with their sons and wives, and even the beasts, birds, and wild animals, assumed divine forms by the grace of Vāsudeva, mounted celestial chariots, and attained the supreme realm, Vaikuṇṭha.
Lord Kṛṣṇa, having bestowed his own disease-free realm upon all the inhabitants of the cowherd station of Nanda, entered the glorious Dvāravatī while being praised by the hosts of gods.
