Worshipped there daily by Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Akrūra, and others, and bearing a universal form, he dallied with his sixteen thousand and eight queens inside bower-dwellings made of divine jewels, upon very soft couches covered with the flowers of celestial trees.

Thus, for the welfare of all the gods and for the destruction of the entire burden of the earth, descending into the Yadu lineage, having destroyed all the demonesses and removed the great burden of the earth, he [delivered] the moving and unmoving beings dwelling in Nanda's Vraja and Dvārikā...
and having established them in the supreme, eternal, and delightful abode meditated upon by yogins, Vāsudeva, constantly served by his divine queens and others, spoke to all:
"The unmanifest Brahman was like water and ghee; / abiding in Prakṛti, released from the guṇas, having liquefied, he went to heaven."

5.77.m: Pārvatī said: / Explain in detail the majesty of the words and meanings of the names, / the essential nature of the Lord, and the glorious manifestations of his abodes;
that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, the various emanations of Hari, / and indeed that which is called nirvāṇa in its essential truth, tell me all, O Lord of gods!

The Lord said: / [Meditation should be done on] Kṛṣṇa in the quintessential Vṛndāvana, surrounded by ten million gopīs; / the Gaṅgā is the supreme power there, and situated therein is the forest of bliss,
fragrant with breezes laden with the perfume of various beautiful flowers, / cooled by the beauty of the divine waves of the daughter of the sun [Yamunā],
touched by the devotees of the Lord, foremost among sages, headed by Sanaka, / adorned by herds of cows with delightful and sweet lowing.
surrounded by dancing boys adorned with lovely garlands and ornaments. / There stands the glorious wish-fulfilling tree, adorned with gold,
abounding in sprouts of various jewels, shining with fruits of various gems. / At its base is an altar of jewels, illuminated by the radiance of gems.
Upon it is an unsurpassed jewel-throne embodying the three Vedas. / Seated there is the Lord of the universe, beyond the three guṇas, imperishable,
resembling ten million moons, brilliant as ten million suns, / having the loveliness of ten million gods of love, illuminating the ten directions,
three-eyed, two-armed, fair, with the radiance of molten gold, / being embraced by women, and ever revered on every side,
meditated upon by Brahmā and others, and by Sanaka and others, subjugated by his devotees; / [surrounded] by women whose eyes are ever rolling, dancing in great festivals,
kissing, laughing, embracing him again and again— / the tens of millions of Vedic verses that have attained the bodies of gopīs,
their minds fixed on the nectar of his lotus feet, surrounded on all sides. / But in their midst is the goddess who has the lustre of molten gold,
shining and making all the directions blaze like lightning, / the sovereign Lady, Pradhāna, by whom all this is pervaded,

who is of the form of creation, preservation, and dissolution, who is knowledge, ignorance, the three Vedas, the supreme, / whose form is intrinsic nature, whose form is power, whose form is Māyā, and who consists of pure consciousness,
the ultimate cause of the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, / by whose Māyā the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings is embraced;
she is called the Queen of Vṛndāvana, Rādhā, because of imitating the Creator. / Having embraced her, dwelling there joyfully is that Lord of Vṛndāvana.
Reeling from intoxication and passion in mutual kissing and embracing— / one should thus meditate on Lord Kṛṣṇa, and he will attain perfection.
The knower of mantras who recites or hears this king of mantras, this secret, / and her mantra as well—that great-souled person is exceedingly rare.
Rādhikā, Citrarekhā, Candrā, Madanasundarī, / Śrīpriyā, Śrīmadhumatī, Śaśirekhā, Haripriyā,
having golden splendour, casting enchantments, adorned with horripilation from love, / accompanied by pallor and perspiration, attached to love, sweet-speaking,
wearing golden garlands, tranquil, delightful, a connoisseur of rasa, / the life of all women, affectionate to the humble, of pure intention,
who has drunk the nectar of the name—she is celebrated as Rādhā, / possessed of a very long smile, with the brilliance of molten gold.
[She is] a fainting river of love, collyrium for the eyes of the choice of Rādhā; / joined with jealousy and delusion, she lives in the empire of the gift [of love].
She is proclaimed Citrarekhā, a battlefield in the festival of amorous dalliance; / fair-limbed, not too tall, and always intent on playing music.
Bewildered by faintness and horripilation from the acting of humility and longing, / she stands at Hari's right side, loving all mantras.
Endowed with the sweet charm of the god of love's desire, she is proclaimed Candrā; / she walks with a graceful, slow gait, her eyes charmingly half-closed.
Overflowing with an effulgent stream of love, radiant as crushed collyrium, / a connoisseur of love for Kṛṣṇa, eager for the sound of the rāsa-dance,
joined with pride, her face reproaching the moon, / skilled in charming speech, the crest-jewel of those who have mastered their senses,
endowed with a beautiful smile—she is indeed Madanasundarī, / delighting in the solitary rāsa-dance, a youthful maiden charming to the dark-hued Lord.
Bewitching Hari's heart with love and an affectionate sidelong glance, / with conquered senses and anger subdued, she is proclaimed his beloved.
Fair-limbed like well-refined gold, beautiful in her playful movement, / her form is sweet with the varied thrill of horripilation born of love's passion.
Endowed with a beautiful smile, her face reproaches the moon; / skilled in charming speech, she is the crest-jewel of those who have conquered their senses.
She is proclaimed Madhumatī, devoted to the practice of love, / accompanied by the fever of bewilderment, horripilation, and a stream of love.
Sporting in the dust of the toll [of love], a great dancer to the music of the rāsa-dance, / she should be known as Śaśirekhā, always beloved of the cowherd boy.
Possessing Kṛṣṇa's very soul, supreme, a youthful maiden with reddish-brown eyes like honey, / occasionally kissed by horripilation through the bewilderment of love for his feet.
In Śivakuṇḍa she is Śivānandā, on the bank of the Dehikā she is Nandinī; / in Dvāravatī she is Rukmiṇī, and in the Vṛndāvana forest she is Rādhā.
In Mathurā she became Devakī, my Supreme Sovereign; / likewise Sītā at Candrakūṭa, and the dweller of the Vindhya mountains in the Vindhyas;
Viśālākṣī in Vārāṇasī, and Vimalā in Puruṣottama. / And the sovereignty of Vṛndāvana was granted to her by Kṛṣṇa when he was pleased with her,
whereas elsewhere the goddess is distinct. But Rādhā is in the forest of Vṛndāvana. / Śauri, whose form is eternal bliss, is said to be bodiless [by the ignorant];
he is described as the presiding deity residing in the limbs of wind, fire, ether, and earth, / and indeed the very form of Govinda is described as [identical to] Brahman.
Just as the sun, though endowed with sense faculties, is not perceived because of its intense splendor, / so Kṛṣṇa, full of brilliance, surely bewilders time.
His form is not material, born of fat, flesh, and bones; / he is the yogin and the Lord, distinct [from nature], the Soul of all, of eternal form.
His solidity is by divine agency, like that of hailstones and clarified butter. / Even the back of the foot of Kṛṣṇa, whose true nature is boundless, is not a [mere created] deity.
In the multitudes of dust particles of Vṛndāvana, there are millions of Viṣṇus; / in the ray of bliss is the moon, having pervaded the universe with its digits.
Just as the nature of the qualities is in the Self, so living beings are the limb-like rays of that [Lord]. / Kṛṣṇa is endowed with two arms; he is never four-armed.
Accompanied by a single cowherd maiden, he sports there always; / Govinda alone is the male, while Brahmā and the other gods are merely women.
Therefore, this is the inherent nature: the Lord is the being beyond nature; / the primordial Male and Nature are Rādhā and the Lord of Vṛndāvana.
All is a transformation of material nature, except the Lord of Vṛndāvana.

This [universe] would arise from origin itself; it has undergone division, for from its destruction / there is no destruction of gold. Just so, even upon the disappearance of the Fish and other incarnations, there is no departure of Kṛṣṇa.
This manifestation of the three qualities and the rest belongs to the one who sports in Vṛndāvana; / it is like the wave of the ocean, whereas the ocean does not become [the wave].
There is no woman equal to Rādhikā, no man equal to Kṛṣṇa; / there is no age beyond youth; his essential nature is beyond material nature.

Youth is to be meditated upon, to be meditated upon; the forest of Vṛndāvana is the forest [above all]; / the dark form alone is the supreme form; the primordial God is the supreme aesthetic experience.
Childhood lasts until the fifth year; boyhood extends up to the tenth; / adolescence is from eight to five [more], its limit extending up to the fifteenth year.
Adolescence burgeoning into youth is called early youth; / that age is his very life; any other age is a worldly manifestation.
I praise that charming age comprising childhood, boyhood, and adolescence, / him who embodies child Gopāla, the cowherd boy, and the love-enchanted Gopāla.
I praise Madanagopāla, wondrous in his adolescent form, / whom they call the glorious Madanamohana, budding with youth.
A great ocean of the joy of undivided, matchless nectar, / triumphant is the hidden body of the Lord of Śrī, having the form of an adolescent boy.

Though he is one, imperishable, primordial, moving in the midst of the cowherd women, / and accessible through meditation, persons of differing minds behold him differently according to the differences in their tastes.
Whose toenail-moon's radiance is Brahman, to be meditated upon by Brahmā and the other gods— / I praise him, the Lord of Vṛndāvana, who has surpassed the three qualities.
There is no departure from Vṛndāvana for Govinda; / whatever form is elsewhere is indeed an artificial manifestation—of this there is no doubt.
Easily attained by the women of Vraja, but difficult to attain by seekers of liberation, / I worship that son of Nanda, the radiance of whose toenails is the supreme mantra.
Pārvatī said: / As long as the demoness of longing for enjoyment and liberation remains in the heart, / how can there arise here the bliss of divine love?
The Lord said: / Well asked by you, O auspicious lady! Whatever is in my mind, / all that I shall tell you; listen attentively.
Remembering his qualities, chanting his name, or singing what delights the mind, / one awakens the self by the self and is constantly absorbed in divine love.

5.78.m: Pārvatī said: / Tell me truly the entire duty of Vaiṣṇavas, / by performing which all men indeed cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
The Lord said: / Now the twelvefold purification of Vaiṣṇavas is declared here: / smearing the floor of [the Lord's] house, and likewise following behind Hari;
circumambulation with devotion, and the cleansing of the feet; / and plucking leaves and flowers with devotion for the worship of Hari;
[this is] for the hands. Among all purifications, this purification is exalted: / chanting his names and also chanting his virtues
with devotion to the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa is considered the purification of speech. / Listening to stories about him and beholding his festivals
are properly declared here as the purification of the ears and the eyes. / Wearing the water washed from his feet, the remnants of his offerings, and his garlands,
is declared the purification of the head bowed before Hari. / Inhaling the fragrance of his flowers and remnants of offerings, O beloved,
would be the purification of the nose within, so it is prescribed. / Whatever flowers and the like are offered to the two feet of Kṛṣṇa,
that alone is the purifier in the world; that indeed purifies everything. / And worship is declared to be fivefold; listen to the distinctions among them from me:
approaching, gathering, devotion, personal recitation of sacred texts, / and sacrifice—the fivefold worship I shall declare to you in order.
There, approaching is the sweeping of the deity's abode, / smearing [with cow dung], and removing the remnants of offerings.
Gathering is the plucking of perfumes, flowers, and the like; / yoga is the contemplation of one's own deity as one's own self with one's own soul.
Svādhyāya is japa preceded by contemplation of the mantra's meaning, / chanting of hymns and praises, and the glorification of Hari;
and study of scriptures on truth and other topics is declared as svādhyāya. / Ijyā is the worship of one's deity according to proper procedure.
Thus the fivefold worship has been told to you, O lady of virtuous vows, / which successively grants equal power, proximity, dwelling in the same world, union, and having the same form.
In this context I shall speak of the worship of the śālagrāma stone / in the sequence of Keśava and the rest, each four-armed, beginning from the upper right hand.
Holding conch, discus, mace, and lotus, he is called Keśava, bearer of the mace; / Nārāyaṇa has the weapons of lotus, mace, discus, and conch respectively.
Mādhava has discus, conch, lotus, and mace; / with mace, lotus, conch, and discus, he is called Govinda, bearer of the mace.
Homage to you in the form of Viṣṇu, holding lotus, conch, discus, and mace; / to the form of Madhusūdana with conch, lotus, mace, and discus.
Homage to Trivikrama endowed with mace, discus, conch, and lotus; / to the Vāmana form with discus, Kaumodakī, lotus, and conch.
Homage to the Śrīdhara form holding discus, lotus, conch, and mace; / O Hṛṣīkeśa, holding discus, mace, conch, and lotus, homage be to you.
To Padmanābha's own form with lotus, conch, mace, and discus; / O Dāmodara, holding conch, mace, discus, and lotus, homage be to you.
Homage to Saṃkarṣaṇa holding conch, lotus, discus, and mace; / O Vāsudeva with discus, conch, mace, and lotus, homage be to you.
To the manifested form of Pradyumna with conch, discus, mace, and lotus; / homage to Aniruddha holding mace, conch, lotus, and discus.
To the form of Puruṣottama with lotus, conch, mace, and discus; / homage to the form of Adhokṣaja holding mace, conch, discus, and lotus.
To the Nṛsiṃha form holding lotus, mace, conch, and discus; / to the Acyuta form holding lotus, discus, conch, and mace, homage be to you.
Homage to the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with mace, lotus, discus, and conch. / The śālagrāma stone having two contiguous discuses situated at the aperture,
with a white-hued line and full of splendor, is the deity Śrī Gadādhara. / When having two contiguous discuses, of reddish hue, with a prominent front part,
it is Saṃkarṣaṇa; next, Pradyumna has a minute discus and is yellowish; / with a very long hollow cavity is Aniruddha, who is circular;
blue and with three lines at the aperture. Next, Nārāyaṇa is black, / with a mace-shaped line in the middle and a very prominent navel lotus.
The one with a broad discus is Nṛsiṃha; the tawny one has three dots; / or rather, the one with five dots is for the worship of a student of sacred lore (brahmacārin).
Varāha is the one with three marks, having two uneven discuses, / blue, with three lines, and thick. Next, the Kūrma form has dots,
black, with a circular whorl, pale, and carrying a back. / Śrīdhara has five lines, wears a forest garland, and is marked with a mace.
The one named Vāmana is circular, with a central discus, and bluish; / the one of diverse colors, many forms, and with serpent coils is Ananta.
Dāmodara is thick, blue, with a discus in the middle, and bluish. / May the one having the opening of Saṃkarṣaṇa protect; next, Brahmā is bright red,
with a very long cavity of lines, one discus, a lotus, and broad; / with a broad discus, a thick opening, black, with a dot, and spotted.
Hayagrīva is hook-shaped, has five lines, and bears the Kaustubha gem; / Vaikuṇṭha appears like a wrestler, consists of a single discus, and is black.
Matsya is shaped like an elongated lotus, has a long line, and is pale; / the one with the Rāma-discus and a line on the right, dark in color, is Trivikrama.
Homage to the mace-bearer residing at Śālagrāma and Dvārakā. / May Sudarśana, bearer of the mace, characterized by one [discus], protect.
Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa is by two, and Trivikrama indeed by three; / Caturvyūha is by four, and Vāsudeva by five.
May Pradyumna protect by six, and Saṃkarṣaṇa by seven; / Puruṣottama is by eight, and Navavyūha is favorable by nine.
Daśāvatāra is by ten; may Aniruddha then protect; / Dvādaśātman is by twelve, and above this it is Ananta.
Brahmā is four-faced, with staff, water-pot, and rosary, prominent; / Maheśvara is five-faced, ten-armed, with the bull on his banner;
according to their weapons, so are Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, / Mahālakṣmī, the Mothers, and the sun god holding a lotus.
And the elephant-faced, the elephant-shouldered, the six-faced, and the many kinds of hosts — / if these are present, installed, or worshipped in a temple,
then dharma, profit, pleasure, and liberation are indeed attained by a man.

5.79.m: The Lord said: / In a śālagrāma, in a gem, in a yantra, in a maṇḍala, and in images / the worship of glorious Hari must be performed daily, but never in a bare building.
In a region of the Gaṇḍakī river lies the great place Śālagrāma; / may the stone produced there, established under the name Śālagrāma, protect.
From touching a śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million births are destroyed; / how much more so worshiping there, which is the cause of Hari’s presence!
From a single sacrifice to a śālagrāma, one obtains the fruit of a hundred liṅgas. / If through merits gained across many births one should obtain a black stone,
bearing the mark of a cow's hoof, through that his rebirth is brought to an end. / First, one should examine the stone: smooth, supreme, and glossy dark-blue;
a blackish one is said to be middling, while a variegated one yields mixed fruits. / Fire, ever residing in wood, is brought to light by churning;
just so all-pervading Hari is perceived in a śālagrāma. / He who daily worships twelve stones of śālagrāma,
joined with a stone from Dvāravatī, is exalted in Vaikuṇṭha. / But if a man spots a cavity in a śālagrāma stone,
his ancestors dwell satisfied in heaven until the end of the kalpa. / Where the Dvāravatī stone is, that place is the abode of Vaikuṇṭha;
he who dies there goes to the city of Viṣṇu, and that sacred place extends for three yojanas. / Recitation, worship, and oblation all become ten-millionfold [in merit].
Whatever desire of the mind one cherishes is fulfilled within the radius of a krośa, without doubt; / because even an insect, when it dies there, goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
The man who sets a price upon a śālagrāma stone, / its seller, its buyer, and he who approves of the examination,
all of them go to hell for as long as the sun and the deluge exist. / Therefore, O goddess, one should avoid buying and selling the disc-marked stone.
The god originating from Śālagrāma and the god originating from Dvārakā — / where the union of the two occurs, liberation is there, without doubt.
Rich in discs originating from Dvārakā, marked with many discs, / having the form of a stone with disc-shaped seats, of the nature of pure consciousness, unstained:
“Homage be to you whose form is the syllable Oṃ, whose nature is eternal bliss! / O greatly fortunate Śālagrāma, show grace to your devotee,
to me who desire your favor and am burdened by debt, O Lord!” / Henceforth I shall joyfully proclaim the rule for the sectarian mark,
hearing which all men may attain similarity of form with Viṣṇu. / One should place Keśava on the forehead, the glorious Puruṣottama on the neck,
the god Nārāyaṇa on the navel, and Vaikuṇṭha on the heart, / Dāmodara on the left side, and Trivikrama on the right,
Hṛṣīkeśa on the crown of the head, and Padmanābha on the back, / the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā on the two ears, and Kṛṣṇa and Hari on the arms.
The deities are declared to be twelve, rejoicing each in its respective place; / one should recite these twelve names while applying the sectarian mark.
With soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. / On whose forehead is seen the vertical mark with upward-going lines,
even an outcaste is pure of soul and worthy of worship indeed, without doubt. / But on the forehead of whatever man the vertical mark is not seen,
one should not look upon him; having seen him, one should gaze upon the sun. / The brāhmaṇa on whom a horizontal mark is seen, and no vertical mark,
after seeing or even touching him, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. / The mark should be made with an interval in the middle, having the shape of Hari's foot.
Whatever lowest of the twice-born should make the vertical mark without a space, / on his forehead there is constantly a dog’s foot, without doubt.
From the nose up to the hair, the vertical mark is very beautiful; / endowed with a gap in the middle, one should know it to be a temple of Hari.
Brahmā resides on the left side, while on the right is Sadāśiva; / one should know Viṣṇu to be in the center, therefore one must not smear the center.
Looking in a mirror or into water, he who carefully applies / the vertical mark, being greatly fortunate, goes to the supreme state.
Fire, the waters, the Vedas, the moon and the sun, and the wind — / all these constantly reside in the right ear of brāhmaṇas.
And the Gaṅgā is in the right ear, and the sacrificial fire in the nose; / simply by touching both, one becomes pure that very moment.
Having poured water into a conch, one should give it, mixed with tulasī, / to high-souled Vaiṣṇavas; one should drink it and revere it with the head bowed,
consume it, and sprinkle his body, sons, friends, and family. / The water from Viṣṇu's feet, when drunk, destroys the sins of ten million births;
that same sin becomes eightfold from letting a drop fall upon the ground. / Holding the water-conch in one's hand, having praised, bowed, and circumambulated,
if that water is kept continuously, by him the fruit of birth has been attained. / In whose house there is no conch or a bell marked with Garuḍa
in front of Vāsudeva, he is no devotee in the Kali age. / Going to the house of the Lord by vehicles or sandals,
and failure to serve during festivals of the god, not bowing before him, / and greeting the Lord when contaminated by food remnants or during ritual impurity;
bowing with only one hand, circumambulating directly in front of him, / stretching out the legs in front, and sitting on a couch,
sleeping, eating, and also speaking falsehood, / loud talking, muttering among themselves, weeping, and quarreling,
punishing and rewarding, and speaking harshly to women, / covering oneself entirely with a garment, blaming others and praising others,
speaking obscenities, releasing downward gas, / offering inferior services despite having the capacity, and eating food not offered to him,
not offering fruits and the like produced in their respective seasons, / offering the remainder of a cooked dish that has already been used,
eating openly, censuring others and praising others, / silence before the teacher, praising oneself, and insulting deities —
these are declared to be the thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu.
“Thousands of offenses are committed day and night by me; / regarding me as ‘I am yours’, forgive them, O Madhusūdana!”
Uttering this mantra, one should bow like a staff upon the ground; / Hari always forgives thousands of transgressions.
Eating at evening and morning as prescribed by the Veda for the twice-born / from what remains after Viṣṇu’s devotee has eaten, one is freed from the sin of the day.
Food is Brahmā, its savor is Viṣṇu: one should eat uttering ‘meat’; / he who eats knowing this is not tainted by the faults of food.
A round bottle-gourd, lentils along with the skin, / a white palmyra fruit, and eggplant: a Vaiṣṇava man should not eat these.
On the leaves of the banyan, holy fig, and swallow-wort, on the leaves of the careya and ebony, / on the mountain-ebony and the kadamba: a Vaiṣṇava man should not eat.
In Śrāvaṇa one should avoid leafy vegetables; in Bhādrapada one should abandon curd; / in the month of Āśvina one should give up milk, and in Kārttika one should abandon meat.
Burnt food, the lime fruit, whatever has not been offered to Viṣṇu, / the citron fruit, leafy greens, and visible salt —
if by chance one should consume them, then one should meditate upon his name. / Winter rice, white, steamed grain, mung beans, sesamum, and barley:
Kalāya peas, kaṅgu millet, wild nīvāra rice, the herb hilamocikā, / kālaśāka, and goosefoot (vāstūka), radish, and red [salt] or other varieties;
among salts, rock salt and sea salt; cow's curd and clarified butter; / milk from which cream has not been extracted; jackfruit, mango, and myrobalan (harītakī);
long pepper, cumin, ginger, orange, tamarind, / plantain, star gooseberry (lavalī), emblic myrobalan (dhātrī) fruits, and sugar-cane products without molasses;
cooked without oil—this the sages declare to be haviṣya food. / Whatever man wears a garland made with tulasī leaves, flowers, and the like,
one should know him to be Viṣṇu himself; this is true, true, there is no doubt. / By planting an emblic myrobalan tree, a man becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
One should know [the sacred area around it] to be Kurukṣetra for three hundred and fifty cubits. / With [beads] carved from tulasī wood made in the shape of rudrākṣa seeds,
having placed the prepared garland around the neck, one should begin the worship; / likewise an āmalaka garland, and properly a puṣkara garland.
A worshipper of Viṣṇu should diligently wear a garland on the neck; / he should also wear the remnant garland of tulasī upon his head.
With sandal paste from the offerings he should mark his body with his names; / and on the forehead the mace should be borne, and on the head the bow and arrow,
and the Nandaka sword in the middle of the heart, the conch and discus on both arms. / If a twice-born marked with the conch and discus dies in a cremation ground,
the destiny that is proclaimed at Prayāga, that destiny is certainly his. / He who, devoted to Viṣṇu, bearing a tulasī leaf upon his head,
performs all ritual actions, obtains imperishable fruit. / Performing an action adorned with garlands of tulasī wood,
what is done for the ancestors and the gods becomes multiplied ten-millionfold. / Having offered to Keśava a garland made of tulasī wood,
when planted, brings about nearness to the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; / when laid at his feet, bestows the fruit of liberation—to that Tulasī, homage!
